look: The first skyscrapers: steel frames, elevators and 20 or more floors, like the Flatiron Building of 1902. Below them, brownstone houses and crowded brick tenements.
Men in suits with bowler hats or straw boaters. Women in long skirts, high-necked blouses and large hats.
Electric streetcars, trains on elevated tracks above the street, horse carts and cabs, and a few early cars. The first subway line opened in October 1904.
Electric signs and lights along Broadway, nicknamed the Great White Way. Many homes still used gas light.
About four million people. Around a million immigrants a year were arriving in the United States, most through Ellis Island.

spots.d: The new home of the New York Times. The square in front of it was renamed Times Square in 1904.
spots.how: The tower still stands, now covered in giant screens.

spots.d: Streetcars ran on rails in the road, powered by electricity.
spots.how: Most of New York's streetcars were gone by the 1950s.

spots.d: The old Met opera house stood on this block of Broadway from 1883 to 1966.
spots.how: Photographs like this are how we know it.

spots.d: Men in hats and women in long skirts on their way to shops and theatres.
spots.how: Count the hats: nearly everyone wears one.

stops.name: The Flatiron Building after a snowstorm
stops.title: Flatiron Building after a snowstorm

spots.d: Finished in 1902, 22 floors on a steel frame. Its triangle shape fits the corner where Broadway crosses Fifth Avenue.
spots.how: It is still one of New York's most famous buildings.

spots.d: Horses still pulled most cabs and wagons.
spots.how: There were far more horses than cars in New York in 1905.

spots.d: After a storm, people walked in paths cut through the drifts in Madison Square.
spots.how: The photograph was taken right after the snow.

stops.name: Herald Square and Macy's
stops.title: Herald Square, facing Macy's, with the elevated railroad

spots.d: The store moved to this corner in 1902 and was one of the biggest shops in the world.
Trains ran on iron tracks above the street, rattling past upstairs windows.
spots.how: This line, the Sixth Avenue El, was taken down in 1938 and 1939.

spots.d: The newspaper building that gave the square its name.
Streetcars, horse wagons and people all share the street.
spots.how: Look closely: there are almost no cars.

stops.name: Mulberry Street
stops.title: Mulberry Street
stops.note: A few years before 1905; the street looked much the same.

spots.d: Pushcarts sold fruit, vegetables, fish and clothes right in the street.
spots.how: The city counted thousands of licensed pushcarts.

spots.d: Five- and six-storey brick buildings with fire escapes on the front. Whole families lived in two or three small rooms.
spots.how: Photographers and reformers of the time recorded these crowded homes.

spots.d: Mulberry Street was the heart of New York's Italian neighbourhood.
spots.how: Italian shops and restaurants still line the street.

spots.d: With tiny homes, children played and worked in the street.
spots.how: You can see dozens of them in this one photograph.
